comparator.name: Human Geography and Planning
comparator.sourceNotes: The adopted 2026–2027 OER B4.2/B4.5 and current dated programme 41220 establish 180 EC: sixty first-year, twenty-four joint second-year research credits plus eighteen Planning and eighteen restricted choices, then eighteen thesis/method credits, twelve thematic and thirty genuinely free credits. The introductory guide paragraph still describes two tracks and twenty-four specialisation credits; the adopted table and actual dated three-branch tree agree on three tracks and eighteen specialisation credits and control. Retain the independently valid existing Planning branch. In year two instantiate Building the City (12 EC) and the separate Planning and Real Estate in Urban Development seminar (6 EC). Retain Moving in the City (12 EC) in year three. Contesting the City is not available in the current year-two thematic list and is not stacked. Select the English Netherlands research project rather than count both language versions. First-year methods follow Thinking Spatially; second-year methods follows Methods 1, and field projects follow specified skills/research-method participation. The thesis needs completed first year, Methods 2 and the Netherlands project, plus participation in Methods 3, normally concurrent. Thirty free credits stay open under approval/enrolment rules; no 30-EC host package, optional internship or destination is invented.
components: Participate in Thinking Spatially before Research Methods 1. The methods sequence combines qualitative and quantitative social research with GIS.
This 12-credit thematic choice examines property-led urban development, land and property markets, regulation and governance. It requires a positive study recommendation or a completed first year.
Seminar: Planning and Real Estate in Urban Development

This separate six-credit seminar examines planning and real-estate actors, negotiation, redevelopment feasibility and residual land value. It is not a six-credit version of Building the City. A positive first-year study recommendation is required.
Pass Research Methods 1 before Research Methods 2. The latter develops GIS, thematic qualitative analysis and multivariable quantitative analysis.

Pass Academic Skills and the Regional Research Project, and meet the participation requirements in Research Methods 2, before this project. A one- to two-week foreign field visit follows preparation in Amsterdam. Destination and theme are selected from the offered projects.

Pass Academic Skills and meet the Research Methods 2 participation requirements. This four-week project includes a full-time residential fieldwork week in the Netherlands, then quantitative survey analysis and thematic analysis of interviews.
The selected Planning specialisation requires this twelve-credit course in the theories and practices of spatial intervention.

The Planning specialisation also requires this six-credit course on professional planning roles, stakeholder and site analysis and alternative policy actions. Earlier planning theory supplies its preparation.
Urban Planning: Moving in the City
The retained twelve-credit thematic choice studies mobility and spatial development. A positive study recommendation or completed first year is required.
Pass Research Methods 2 and the Netherlands Research Project before Research Methods 3. This course develops the research design and proposal and is normally taken alongside the thesis.

Thirty credits remain open for university bachelor courses, a minor, an approved exchange or an approved internship. Study must take place while enrolled in the degree; vocational higher-education courses do not count. Other arrangements require Examination Board approval.
Bachelor Thesis Project Human Geography & Planning

The twelve-credit thesis is an individual original research project in human geography or planning, supervised within a thematic project group. Pass all first-year courses, Research Methods 2 and the Netherlands Research Project, and meet the participation requirement in Research Methods 3. The latter may run alongside the thesis.

routeSelection.basis: Retain the already selected coherent Planning specialisation, verified in the adopted current OER and dated branch, independently of UCR fit. A changed catalogue order is not reason to discard a valid route. The former year-two Contesting/Building combination is invalid under the current menu: choose the actual twelve-credit Building thematic and its coherent six-credit Planning/Real Estate seminar. The valid prior Moving thematic is retained in year three.

alternatives.label: People, places & spatial sustainability
alternatives.concept: Investigate how communities, institutions and environmental change shape places. Social theory, public economics, governance and policy analysis connect to climate, water adaptation, GIS and environmental evidence, supported by qualitative and quantitative research and partner-based sustainability inquiry.
alternatives.labelReason: Investigate how communities, institutions and environmental change shape places. Social theory, public economics, governance and policy analysis connect to climate, water adaptation, GIS and environmental evidence, supported by qualitative and quantitative research and partner-based sustainability inquiry.
progression: Formal prerequisites and actual covered-term offerings pass. Social and political foundations precede advanced theory where feasible. Partner-based Research in a Sustainable Delta has no formal prerequisite and is planned only in 2026h2; its first-year placement is acknowledged rather than inventing a later offering or a hard prerequisite.
alternatives.distinctness: Public Economics and Public Policy Analysis replace materials/recovery laboratories, strengthening concrete social and institutional inquiry while retaining GIS, water and climate foundations.

alternatives.label: Urban governance, inequality & policy
alternatives.concept: Investigate inclusive public decisions through social inequality, political and legal institutions, public economics, group behaviour and sustainability governance. Qualitative research, survey design, rights, property law, climate communication and policy persuasion supply specific tools for analysing collective choices affecting cities and communities.
alternatives.labelReason: Investigate inclusive public decisions through social inequality, political and legal institutions, public economics, group behaviour and sustainability governance. Qualitative research, survey design, rights, property law, climate communication and policy persuasion supply specific tools for analysing collective choices affecting cities and communities.
alternatives.distinctness: Replaces most Earth-system/GIS work with rights, constitutional/private law, institutions, public economics, social research and policy communication. Product design is replaced by substantive public economics.
progression: Formal prerequisites and actual covered-term offerings pass. Social and political foundations precede advanced theory where feasible. Partner-based Research in a Sustainable Delta has no formal prerequisite and is planned only in 2026h2; its first-year placement is acknowledged rather than inventing a later offering or a hard prerequisite.

alternatives.label: Global connections, identity & place
alternatives.concept: Investigate how empire, international institutions, economic connections, race, Indigenous histories and cultural exchange shape identity and place. Social theory, qualitative inquiry, historical research, Mediterranean and African heritage and public-law frameworks connect local experiences to wider systems.
alternatives.labelReason: Investigate how empire, international institutions, economic connections, race, Indigenous histories and cultural exchange shape identity and place. Social theory, qualitative inquiry, historical research, Mediterranean and African heritage and public-law frameworks connect local experiences to wider systems.
alternatives.distinctness: Replaces spatial environmental and domestic policy priorities with imperial/Indigenous histories, Mediterranean/African heritage, international law and social identity. General social psychology replaces youth-extremism education; migration is not claimed as an independently taught sequence.
progression: Formal prerequisites and actual covered-term offerings pass. Social and political foundations precede advanced theory where feasible. Partner-based Research in a Sustainable Delta has no formal prerequisite and is planned only in 2026h2; its first-year placement is acknowledged rather than inventing a later offering or a hard prerequisite.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: Human geography and spatial planning: how people, institutions and environments shape places across scales
Urban life, housing, mobility, inequality and inclusive city development
Spatial, quantitative and qualitative research using GIS, statistics, surveys, interviews, observation and fieldwork
Planning theory, spatial interventions, stakeholder analysis, governance and practical solution development
Independent place-based research culminating in a bachelor thesis
adjacent: Human geography through social relations, migration, inequality, political economy and regional development
Global urbanism and transnational planning through global connections, mobility and cross-border governance
Spatial sustainability through climate change, water, environmental systems and the built environment
questions: How can cities and regions become more sustainable, inclusive and resilient?
How do political institutions, economies and social power shape spatial development and everyday urban life?
How can spatial data, field research and stakeholder evidence support defensible planning decisions?

trace: Mandatory first-year academic writing, source evaluation, research-literacy, reflective development and civic collaboration.
Provides economic concepts for land, housing, regional development and urban change.
Explains international economic linkages and shocks that connect regional and global development.

Direct welfare/public-policy analysis through public goods, externalities, redistribution, tax/spending, model/evidence evaluation and a research proposal/paper; complements collective local-policy decisions.
Provides regression-based quantitative analysis for relationships among economic, social and spatial outcomes.
Provides quantitative research design and statistics for analysing social and spatial patterns.
Complementary psychological safety, minority inclusion and leadership under conflict plus a supervised quantitative survey/data-analysis project; not a general urban-diversity curriculum.
Introduces computational data handling and visualisation for evidence about places and populations.
Direct place-based analysis of water risks, infrastructure, history, governance and justice in Zeeland, with site inquiry and context-sensitive adaptation.
Analyses institutions, stakeholders and policy choices in environmental governance.
Direct geospatial methods: ArcGIS Pro, vector/raster data models, projections, georeferencing, queries, transformations, surfaces and remote sensing applied to environmental change.
Complementary Earth-system models, climate proxies/isotope tracers and greenhouse-gas field investigation; no invented urban/social data analysis.
Complementary physical/chemical Earth-system foundation for climate and environmental geospatial work, including dynamic models; not a human-geography course.
Explains climate processes, impacts and adaptation questions central to spatial futures.

Direct partner-based sustainability research in the Zeeland delta, with literature, question, design, investigation and report/product; specific topic and techniques depend on the partner and are not guaranteed urban field methods.
Introduces legal, social and normative analysis of institutions governing everyday life.
Historicises empire and the uneven global relations that have shaped regions and mobility.
Studies Indigenous place, power and community through histories shaped by settler colonialism.
Direct historical research-question/source-criticism/interdisciplinary paper methods in the current American Century course; the excluded Walcheren outline is not used.
Examines rights and justice claims relevant to exclusion, inequality and inclusive cities.
Provides the international legal frame through which states, borders and transnational issues operate.
Compares constitutional and administrative structures through which public interventions are authorised.
Complementary property, tort and contract analysis with comparative cases and mediation; no unsupported claim that it teaches tenancy or housing-policy specialisation.
Builds comparative analysis of political institutions and their effects on public decisions.
Explains globalisation, geopolitics and relations that connect places across borders.
Examines multilevel European governance that materially shapes regions and cities.
Direct public-policy process and memo methods using a global sugar-policy case; complementary policy reasoning rather than a dedicated urban planning studio.
Direct interdisciplinary conflict/identity/structural-inequality analysis and evidence-based policy briefs; specific support to collective decisions, not presumed migration training.
Introduces the concepts and scales needed to analyse people, institutions and societies in place.
Develops interviewing, ethnographic observation, coding and reflexive qualitative inquiry.
Provides modern sociological theories for interpreting inequality, identity and social change.
Connects collective action, environmental justice and unequal exposure to spatial-environmental harms.
Engages advanced contemporary debates about power, institutions and changing societies.
Complementary social cognition, prejudice, groups, social influence and research-design literacy for understanding how identities and settings shape community life.
Analyses how climate claims and urban-environmental futures are publicly framed and contested.
Develops evidence-based persuasion for communicating policy and planning proposals.
Direct African visual/heritage inquiry with colonial collecting, restitution and cross-cultural modernism; specific place/cultural ownership contribution, not global planning.

Direct historically grounded cultural connections through Renaissance Mediterranean trade, colonialism, architecture and artistic exchanges across Europe, Africa, Asia and the Americas; not a contemporary migration course.
Examines how racial power, privilege and resistance are represented in public culture.
blocks: People, institutions, spatial evidence and applied inquiry
Both develop source evaluation, academic writing, research integrity, reflection and collaborative learning. UvA additionally introduces geographical academic practice and interview skills.

Both introduce research design, statistics, empirical data and survey/experimental reasoning. UvA combines this with introductory interviews and socio-spatial questions; UCR develops a full empirical project.

Both conduct supervised survey research, analyse original data and report findings. UvA also requires residential spatial fieldwork and thematic interview analysis; UCR centres psychological inclusion and leadership.

Both connect environmental pressures, infrastructure and institutions to changing places. UCR centres adaptation and water governance in Zeeland; UvA studies a wider range of Amsterdam urban dynamics, including housing and mobility.

Both analyse institutions, participation, conflict and collective interventions. UvA develops dedicated spatial-planning theories and urban interventions; UCR centres sustainability governance and policy advice.
Both use ArcGIS Pro and spatial data/models to create and analyse maps. UvA also introduces social-scientific research philosophy and ethics; UCR adds environmental remote sensing.

Both formulate questions and conduct collaborative applied research with external stakeholders. UvA specifically develops a regional urban vision and stakeholder roles; UCR projects concern a partner-defined sustainability problem and do not guarantee a planning studio.

Both connect research questions, theory, evidence, methods and ethical reflection in a research/policy design. UvA specifically prepares the individual geography/planning thesis; UCR produces interdisciplinary conflict-policy research and a brief.
Both study social relations, institutions and inequality. UvA specifically organises these around place, space, scales and geographical traditions; UCR supplies general sociological frameworks.
Both develop interviews, observation, qualitative research design, coding and thematic interpretation. UvA additionally integrates GIS and multivariable quantitative analysis.
Related knowledge appears in selected courses, but no additional course is counted as this dedicated geography/planning component.
Property, institutions and economic policy contribute relevant foundations, but there is no dedicated property-led urban-development course.
No selected course centres real-estate development feasibility, residual land value and urban redevelopment negotiation.
No selected course guarantees supervised research with an overseas field visit and its specific cross-context reflection.
Related knowledge appears in selected courses, but no additional course is counted as this dedicated geography/planning component.
No selected course centres the dedicated transport, accessibility and urban-mobility sequence.
The external thirty-credit elective space remains genuinely open within university-level, enrolment and approval rules.
The individual original geography/planning thesis remains compulsory. Optional UCR independent research is additional to scheduled 180 credits.

selection.assessment: The closest programme integrates the target’s social-spatial, environmental and mixed-method core. The Human Geography and Global Urbanism directions are separately evidenced by official specialisations and produce materially different governance/inequality and transnational-place curricula. All three are mechanically feasible and pairwise differ by at least nine courses, so production stops at the three-alternative maximum.

notes.text: UCR combines social, political and environmental inquiry with research methods and specific studies of place. UvA provides a sustained geography and planning sequence, dedicated urban/property/mobility subjects, field projects and an individual thesis. The course relationships shown are partial.

audience.programmeDescription: Human Geography and Planning at the University of Amsterdam examines how people, institutions and environments shape places. This example follows Planning, with Building the City and its separate Planning and Real Estate seminar in year two, and Moving in the City in year three.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR can emphasise people and spatial sustainability, public governance and inequality, or global connections, identity and place. These options combine relevant social, environmental and research subjects. UvA offers more sustained geographical theory, urban and property planning, mobility and supervised field research. The relationships shown are partial.
